# Pauli's egg dream — spontaneous division, conscious participation and the circle

## #0 — A physicist meets his concepts in a dream

Pauli's egg dream is a sequence of seven pictures. A woman arrives with a bird; an egg is laid and divides; the dreamer discovers another egg in his own hand and participates in its division; the four eggs become mathematical expressions; his spoken recognition is followed by a circle. The whole depends upon who acts at each stage and upon the changes between image, operation, formula and speech. Its source is Pauli's own account in **“Modern Examples of ‘Background Physics’,” Appendix 3, section 4**, in *Atom and Archetype*, printed pp. 192–196. The [Jung–Pauli source house](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype/jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype.md) **sources** the work identity and admitted consulted-carrier paraphrases `jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype-p001` (telling) and `p002` (commentary); the local Princeton-imprint, David Roscoe translation supplies the primary text. The house's selected Routledge 2001 carrier remains a separate edition-collation task.

Markus Fierz's accompanying note, Appendix 2, pp. 176–178, describes an undated typescript found among the correspondence and characterises it as an outline rather than a finished publication. Pauli introduces “background physics” as physical concepts appearing spontaneously in dreams in a qualitative, symbolic sense. He initially finds such usage offensive to his scientific habits. His subsequent inquiry concerns both the psychic activity of these images and the archetypal background of scientific concepts. He explicitly distinguishes that inquiry from a formulated body of scientific truths. The egg therefore enters through a physicist receiving his own disciplinary language in a mode he did not consciously choose. (Appendix 3, pp. 179–180.)

Pauli places two related dreams within an interval of four days in the middle of March, when his work on Kepler had largely come to an end. The appendix supplies no calendar year there. Pauli’s later **60P, Zürich, 31 March 1953, p.107 and footnote 9**, identifies the first dream as 1948 and the background-physics essay as June 1948, followed by the quaternity dream. The [dating passage](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype/jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype.md#jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype-p006) **sources** this witness. Mid-March 1948 for the pair follows by cross-reference; no exact day is supplied. Fierz’s description of the surviving typescript as undated remains distinct from this retrospective dating. Pauli's equinox association is his own retrospective account of relative psychic instability and creativity. The egg dream names no city, room or landscape. Its space is enacted by arrival, approach and the discovery of something already in the dreamer's hand. **Göttingen belongs to the companion dream**, where his first physics teacher announces a fundamental change in the splitting of the hydrogen atom's ground state, speaks of brass tones engraved on a metal plate, and the dreamer then goes to Göttingen. Pauli's later interpretation connects that destination with mathematics as well as physics. The two dreams belong together in his account, but their scenes remain distinct. (Pp. 192, 194.)

This whole's production world is Pauli's physicist-led inquiry in the Jung–Pauli correspondence, subsequently preserved in an edited collection. Its narrated time is the seven-picture succession; its biographical time is the reported mid-March pair; its later publication and project reception have their own histories. The World Clock is another image and supplies no missing scene here.

## #1 — The first division happens before the dreamer intervenes

**Picture 1.** A woman comes with a bird. The bird lays a large egg. The account gives neither the woman's name nor the bird's species. Their action brings the egg into the dream; it does not identify the woman as a particular goddess or mother, or the bird as a named mythological creature. The first diagram shows the single egg. Its enclosing outline is still the form of one thing awaiting what will happen to it.

**Picture 2.** The egg divides itself into two. Pauli's grammatical distinction matters: this division occurs without his reported intervention. The ensuing diagram places two complete egg outlines beside one another. The dream has made a plurality from its first egg before it makes the dreamer's own agency visible. The two are not described as a good egg and an evil egg, and no conflict occurs between them. What changes is the field of the image: one has become two while each remains presented as an egg. (Pp. 192–193.)

The woman and bird are not given further actions in the telling. Their contribution remains the arrival and laying through which the scene began. Nothing in the later formula retroactively supplies them with a historical identity. The source preserves a sequence of events whose significance can be explored without filling its unnamed figures with borrowed narrative.

## #2 — The dreamer finds what is in his own hand

**Picture 3.** Pauli goes closer. He notices that he has another egg in his hand, this one with a blue shell. His approach changes what he recognises within the situation: alongside the two that divided spontaneously there is now a third, already held by the observer. The account does not say that he manufactures it or takes it from the first pair. The diagram retains the two above and adds the third beneath them. The additional egg changes both the number of visible terms and the dreamer's position among them.

**Picture 4.** He divides this last egg into two. They miraculously remain whole, and he now has two blue-shelled eggs. His action differs from the first egg's self-division. The scene has passed from watching a division to performing one upon what he holds. The fourth diagram shows two pairs. The source records preservation through this division as the marvel: the result is two eggs, not two broken portions requiring an invented repair. It gives no hatching, birth of a creature, discarded shell or yolk. (P. 193.)

The two pairs have related but distinct histories. One results from a spontaneous change witnessed by Pauli; the other follows his recognition and action. Wholeness has survived both passages into plurality. This is the event on which his later commentary concentrates: conscious intervention enters a situation whose first terms were already given. Its force would disappear if the four eggs were introduced at once as an emblem with four fixed meanings.

## #3 — Four eggs become a relation, and the relation becomes a circle

<a id="pauli-egg-seven-pictures"></a>
**Picture 5.** The four eggs change into four mathematical expressions. Pauli's printed arrangement has two rows, each containing a cosine term on the left and a sine term on the right:

$$
\begin{matrix}
\cos(\delta/2) & \sin(\delta/2)\\
\cos(\delta/2) & \sin(\delta/2)
\end{matrix}
$$

The duplicated terms preserve the paired arrangement while changing the medium in which the scene is presented. The picture reports this transformation directly. It does not explicitly assign each shell colour to a particular trigonometric function, so no such assignment is added here.

**Picture 6.** The terms give the quotient

$$
\frac{\cos(\delta/2)+i\sin(\delta/2)}
     {\cos(\delta/2)-i\sin(\delta/2)}.
$$

The two rows now form a relation of conjugate expressions: the cosine remains the same while the imaginary sine term changes sign. For real \(\delta\), the denominator has modulus one. The quotient is an ordinary, well-defined complex-number operation. The dream's organisation has changed from four displayed terms into a single relation that retains their opposing signs.

**Picture 7.** Pauli speaks for the first time in this dream. He identifies the expression with \(e^{i\delta}\) and names the circle. The formula vanishes and a circle appears. This replacement completes the reported sequence. Speech enters at the end, after the silent pictures have changed the observer's participation and the form of what is seen. (P. 193; diagrams visually checked in the consulted PDF.)

Pauli's subsequent explanation makes the mathematical step explicit:

$$
\frac{\cos(\delta/2)+i\sin(\delta/2)}
     {\cos(\delta/2)-i\sin(\delta/2)}
=\frac{e^{i\delta/2}}{e^{-i\delta/2}}
=e^{i\delta}.
$$

For a fixed real angle this is a point on the unit circle; as the angle varies it describes the circle. The distinction keeps the mathematical operation exact while preserving what Pauli recognises in the dream. The final image is circular rather than the initial egg outline. The account reports neither a return of the woman and bird nor a restart of the first picture. Its completion has the history of differentiation and conscious action within it; no unreported eighth scene is needed.

## #4 — Pauli reads the part played by consciousness

Pauli's commentary joins the two dreams through the intervention absent from the initial pair of eggs. He reads that spontaneous pair as a ground state, then identifies his participation in Pictures 3 and 4 as the change that produces the quaternity through a reflection of duality. In his account the second dream goes beyond the first: it makes the intervention pictorially explicit and carries the result into mathematical wholeness. He relates the sequence to the axiom attributed to Maria Prophetissa, mediated here through Jung's *Psychology and Alchemy*. That is Pauli's comparison, not an independently verified ancient attribution. (P. 195.)

He also gives the imaginary unit a symbolic office. Its introduction permits the paired opposites to combine into the form he reads as wholeness. Mathematics, for him, already participates in symbolic description; the distinction at issue is what such description can embrace. He refuses to present a finished interpretation of the two dreams and writes that further progress in the sciences would be required. His refusal leaves his actual interpretation of conscious intervention, quaternity and mathematical unity fully available; it limits the claim that the dreams' entire meaning has been exhausted.

The surrounding essay gives that boundary practical content. Pauli distinguishes a physical process from its psychic symbolic use: a faster process is not thereby more conscious, nor does a heavier atom have more consciousness than a lighter one. At the end he distinguishes the limits of physics within life from an alleged defect of quantum theory within physics. Feeling, judgment and the individual case have an office that reproducible quantitative description does not by itself perform. Mathematics also has qualitative resources, including topology, whose symbolic possibilities he considers unfinished. The dream's formula is mathematically exact while the scope of its psychological meaning remains an inquiry. (Pp. 190, 195–196.)

[Neumann's complete round–differentiation–transformation movement](../../../archetypal-ground/neumann-images/WHOLE.md) **compares** the shared archetypal structuration through which a containing form gives rise to differentiated terms and a centre capable of participation. The [Neumann source house](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/neumann/neumann-1954-origins-history-consciousness/neumann-1954-origins-history-consciousness.md) **sources** that separate morphology; its protected encounter retains Taylor's own paper/mark/slash/erasure and eightfold readings. In the egg dream, the centre enters through noticing and dividing what it already holds. Its mathematical end and its specific paired actions belong to Pauli's telling. Neumann's world parents, hero and uroboros do not become extra characters in that dream. **Human-amplified: no** for a new exact egg-to-Neumann stage assignment; the shared-ground comparison supplies orientation rather than a substitute narrative.
